newsitem.title: FRANCE: French group sues Le Pen over gas chamber remark.
newsitem.headline: French group sues Le Pen over gas chamber remark.

text.p: An anti-racist group said on Monday it would sue French far-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen for saying gas chambers had nothing to do with anti-semitism and repeating they were a mere detail of World War Two.

France's Movement against Racism MRAP said Le Pen's comment, in an interview to the U.S. news magazine New Yorker, following his espousal of racial inequality, was part of "a deliberate strategy of inciting racial hatred".
"MRAP solemnly requires the justice minister to start legal proceedings against Jean-Marie Le Pen. For its part it intends to assume its responsibilities by taking court action," it said.
The New Yorker asked Le Pen about his 1987 comment that Nazi gas chambers were a mere detail in wartime history.
Le Pen's reply was: "The gas chambers have nothing to do with anti-semitism. When I say that the gas chambers are a detail of the history of the Second World War, it's obvious.

"If you take a book on the Second World War of a thousand pages, you will have four pages on deportation (to concentration camps), and on these four pages you have six lines on the gas chambers," he said.
Le Pen was taken to court in France over his 1987 statement and ordered to pay heavy damages to war victims' groups.
Henri Hadjenberg, president of the Council of French Jewish Institutions (CRIF), French Jewry's umbrella organisation, said he hoped Le Pen would be prosecuted over his latest comments.
"We condemn this new provocation and hope the French justice system will itself initiate legal action on this provocation," Hadjenberg told French radio.
He also voiced outrage at a comparison Le Pen made between Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Adolf Hitler.
"If it's national and patriotic ideology that is the basis of Nazism, then Netanyahu is a super-Hitler," Le Pen said.

Le Pen caused an outcry recently by saying that racial inequality was "a fact". Justice Minister Jacques Toubon said he could not prosecute him over that comment because it was too vague to come under French law punishing racist attacks against specific groups or individuals.
Toubon proposed instead to tighten the anti-racism laws, but the plan was dropped as some saw it as double-edged and a threat to freedom of expression.
Denying being a racist, Le Pen also told the New Yorker: "What do I have to do not to be racist? Marry a black woman? With AIDS if possible?"

CRIF said in a separate statement that Le Pen's comments appeared aimed at drawing attention to himself as France headed for a snap parliamentary election which President Jacques Chirac was expected to announce later on Monday.
"To get back up there into print, Jean-Marie Le Pen is coming back to one of his favourite themes: Jews," CRIF said.
Le Pen scored nearly 15 percent in the country's 1995 presidential elections and his party is expected to chalk up a similar score if parliamentary elections were held now.
